Loading packages

library(palmerpenguins)
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
library(knitr)

The ggplot2 package

Its the most popular Data Visualization package in R.

ggplot2 Structure of code

The structure of the code for ggplot2 objects is of the form:

” ggplot(data = [dataset],
      mapping = aes(x = [x-variable],
                    y = [y-variable] )) +
  geom_xxx() +
  other options ”

Example: Palmer Penguins data

The Palmer Penguins data set contains data on 344 penguins from 3 islands in Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.

Palmer penguins data summary

Variable Description
species Species of the penguin
island Island the penguin was found on
bill_length_mm Bill length (mm)
bill_depth_mm Bill depth (mm)
flipper_length_mm Flipper length (mm)
body_mass_g Body mass (g)
sex Sex of the penguin
year Year data was collected

➡️ First, let’s load the Palmer Penguins data set and explore some high-level characteristics of the data set using the code below:

data(penguins, package = "palmerpenguins")

we can glimpse our data to start. (In R, glimpse() is a function from the dplyr package (part of the tidyverse) that gives you a quick, transposed preview of your dataset ).

glimpse(penguins)
Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species           <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adel…
$ island            <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgerse…
$ bill_length_mm    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, …
$ bill_depth_mm     <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 18.1, …
$ flipper_length_mm <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186…
$ body_mass_g       <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, …
$ sex               <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, female, male…
$ year              <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…

Activity1:

ggplot2 data visualization steps

visualizing the relationship between the bill depth of the penguins (mm) and the bill lengths (mm) of the penguins.

aesthetics is used in data visualizations to differentiate between subgroups or to show additional dimensions of the data by mapping characteristics to a variable such as color, shape or size.

Plot in layers

i_ making a blank canvas for our visualization using the penguins data frame.

ii_ adding bill depth to the x-axis.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x=bill_depth_mm)   )

iii_ adding bill length to the y-axis.

penguins |>
  ggplot( aes(x=bill_depth_mm, y=bill_length_mm  ) )

iv_ adding points using geom_point() to the plot to create scatter plot. (Additional layers are added to a ggplot using the + operator).

penguins |>
  ggplot( aes(x=bill_depth_mm, y=bill_length_mm) )+
  geom_point()

v_ adding color to the points using color() in our scatter plot based on the species of the penguin being Adelie, Chinstrap, or Gentoo, reproducing the plot below.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x=bill_depth_mm,
             y=bill_length_mm,
             color= species))+
geom_point()

vi_ adding another layer to our ggplot to customize the Title and Subtitle using the labs() function to reproduce the plot below.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x=bill_depth_mm,
             y=bill_length_mm,
             color= species))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(title="Penguin bill length by bill depth",
       subtitle = "Dimensions for Adelie, chinstrap, and Gentoo Penguins")

Activity2:

ggplot2 customization

i_ ➡️ Customizing the axis labels using the x and y options in the labs() function.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x=bill_depth_mm,
             y=bill_length_mm,
             color= species))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(title="Penguin bill length by bill depth",
       subtitle = "Dimensions for Adelie, chinstrap, and Gentoo Penguins",
       x="bill depth(mm)",
       y="bill length(mm)" )

ii_ ➡️ Customize the legend title to be “Species” instead of “species”

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x=bill_depth_mm,
             y=bill_length_mm,
             color= species))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(title="Penguin bill length by bill depth",
       subtitle = "Dimensions for Adelie, chinstrap, and Gentoo Penguins",
       x="bill depth(mm)",
       y="bill length(mm)",
       color= "Species")

iii_ ➡️ Adding caption which may explain source of data

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x=bill_depth_mm,
             y=bill_length_mm,
             color= species))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(title="Penguin bill length by bill depth",
       subtitle = "Dimensions for Adelie, chinstrap, and Gentoo Penguins",
       x="bill depth(mm)",
       y="bill length(mm)",
       color= "Species",
       caption = "Source:Station LTER / polmernguins packag" )

iii_ ➡️ Lastly, use a discrete color scale that is inclusive of viewers with common forms of color blindness by adding a scale_color_viridis_d() layer to the plot, creating the final plot below.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x=bill_depth_mm,
             y=bill_length_mm,
             color= species))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(title="Penguin bill length by bill depth",
       subtitle = "Dimensions for Adelie, chinstrap, and Gentoo Penguins",
       x="bill_depth(mm)",
       y="bill_length(mm)",
       color="Species",
       caption = "Source:Station LTER / polmernguins packag") +
  scale_color_viridis_d()

Congrats! 🎨 🎉 🥳 now created a visualization using ggplot2!

Mapping vs Setting

Mapping in ggplot2 is the process of using aesthetics in a visualization to show additional variables from a data set

For example, in the plot below, body_mass_g is mapped to the size aesthetic.

i_ mapping body_mass_g to the size aesthetic.

When we say body_mass_g is mapped to the size aesthetic, it means that the visual size of each dot on the plot is determined by how heavy that individual penguin is.

ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = bill_depth_mm,
           y = bill_length_mm,
           size = body_mass_g)) + 
  geom_point()

ii_ mapping flipper_length_mm to the alpha aesthetic.

When we say flipper_length_mm is mapped to the alpha aesthetic, it means that the transparency of each dot on the plot is determined by the length of that penguin’s flippers.

ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = bill_depth_mm,
           y = bill_length_mm,
           size = body_mass_g,
           alpha= flipper_length_mm)) + 
  geom_point()

Setting

Setting in ggplot2 is the process of manually specifying aesthetics for a visualization based on fixed values for all observations.

i_ set the value of aesthetic to 2

When we say size = 2 sets the value of the aesthetic, it means you are manually forcing every single dot on the plot to have a fixed, identical size, completely ignoring any variables in the data.

ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = bill_depth_mm,
           y = bill_length_mm)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2)

ii_ Reproduce the plot below by also setting the alpha aesthetic to be 0.50.

ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = bill_depth_mm,
           y = bill_length_mm)) + 
  geom_point(size = 0.50)

Question 2:

➡️ Reproduce the histogram of the penguin body masses displayed below using ggplot2. Hint: we can control the outline color of the bars in the histogram using the color aesthetic.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "white", position = "identity", alpha = 0.5, ) +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin body masses",
    x = "Body Mass (g)",
    y = "Frequency",
    color = "Species",
    caption = "Source: Palmer Station LTER / palmerpenguins package") +
  scale_color_viridis_d()

Question 3:

➡️ Reproduce the box plot of the penguin body masses displayed below using ggplot2. Hint: to suppress the y-axis text and ticks, add a theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) layer to the plot.

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             color = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin body masses",
    x = "Body Mass (g)",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Species",
    fill = "Species",
    caption = "Source: Palmer Station LTER / palmerpenguins package"
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(), 
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )
